new_statements.quote: I have spent a lot of time learning Ibisi but I really did not become a speaker. This language has tones that give different meaning to word with the same pronunciation. To learn these tones , we knocked on glasses of water that resonated with high, middle or low sound which was transcribed on the written syllables. [...] In these texts, I did not write the words with their tones ( I am not a linguist and I have forgotten most of what I have learned!) but only basic English linguistic sounds, some with a phonetic sign.

In: Piti Abisi Kaduna Nigeria - Cultural History (the author's English-language web memoir of his 1973 ethnographic fieldwork among the Abisi/Piti, Universite Laval anthropologist, author of the 1976-1983 Abisi ethnographic corpus listed in PRIOR). pitiabisi.wordpress.com.
new_statements.locator: web page '1 Who am I? Why write about Piti Abisi?', section headed 'Writing Abisi Language' (paragraphs 1, 2 and 4 of that section; lines 23-27 of the saved text extract)
new_statements.relation_note: A non-linguist fieldworker's first-hand statement that Abisi (Piti) is a tone language in which pitch distinguishes otherwise identical words, learned and transcribed with three pitch levels (high, middle, low) marked on syllables; he adds that the Abisi words in his texts are written without tones. Nothing on stress or accent. This agrees with the three level diacritics (acute/macron/grave) used throughout the 2013 SIL Piti/Riban survey wordlist (A's work 1). It is a memoir remark, not an analysis: no tone inventory argument, no minimal pairs given, no statement on contours or downstep.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical tone: words with identical segments differ in meaning by tone; three pitch levels (high, mid, low) were distinguished in the author's 1973 transcription.
new_statements.identity_note: The Abisi (self-name; language called 'Ibisi' by the author, cf. Blench's Ibishi/Bishi) of 'Piti', Kaduna State, with Mambo and Kirat villages, Ribam (Riban) neighbours, Rukuba/Kurama contacts and the Sarkin Piti - the same community as Glottolog piti1243 Piti/Bishi (pcn), Lere LGA; Chalifoux is the ethnographer whose 'Abisi (Piti)' articles pass 1 already identified. First-hand: he spent 1973 in Abisi learning the language.
